ai_summary: Scotland’s electricity system is currently operating at an exceptional 0 gCO2/kWh carbon intensity, contrasting sharply with the 128 gCO2/kWh recorded GB-wide. Across Great Britain, total GB wind output stands at 7.8 GW, with estimated Scottish wind output contributing 1.2 GW, representing 11.9% of installed Scottish wind capacity. Despite these clean generation conditions, structural grid transmission bottlenecks between Scotland and major southern demand centres prevent full utilisation. So far today, 578 MWh of Scottish generation has been curtailed through Balancing Mechanism bids, incurring a constraint cost of about £38,660. To balance the shortfall, thermal generators were dispatched elsewhere on the network, leading to an estimated 109,820 m3 of gas burned elsewhere and emitting 202 tonnes of CO2. Annualising today's figures indicates an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of £14 million, which increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £0.05/MWh across total national electricity demand. This operational friction underscores how cross-border transmission limitations directly compromise carbon abatement by substituting zero-carbon Scottish wind with fossil generation, while simultaneously imposing preventable balancing expenses onto UK billpayers.
